'''Kawahíva''' (Kawahíb, Kagwahib) is a [[Tupi–Guarani]] [[dialect cluster]] of [[Brazil]].

The [[Tenharim]] (self-designation, {{lang|pah|Pyri}} 'near, together'), [[Parintintín]], Jiahúi, [[Amondawa]], [[Karipúna]],{{efn|not to be confused with either the [[Chacobo language|Panoan group]] or the [[Karipúna French Creole|Carib-based creole]] spoken in the state of Amapá, which have the same name.}} [[Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau dialect|Uru-eu-wau-wau]] (self-designation {{lang|urz|Jupaú}}), [[Piripkura|Piripkúra]], [[Juma people|Júma]], and Capivarí all call themselves ''Kawahíva''. Their speech is mutually intelligible, and also similar with other languages or dialects now extinct. The closest Tupí-Guaraní language seems to be [[Apiaká language|Apiaká]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hammarström |first=Harald |date=September 2015 |title=Ethnologue 16/17/18th editions: A comprehensive review: Online appendices |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/593411 |journal=Language |language=en |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=s1–s188 |doi=10.1353/lan.2015.0049 |issn=1535-0665}}</ref> formerly spoken in Mato Grosso.

==Varieties==
There are different internal classifications of the pan-Kawahíwa, which differ in, e.g., whether Kayabí and Apiaká should be included as part of the dialectal cluster. The one listed in Aguilar (2013, 2018) follows:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aguilar |first1=Ana Maria Gouveia Cavalcanti |title=Kawahíwa como uma unidade linguística |journal=Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica |date=2018 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=139–161 |doi=10.26512/rbla.v9i1.19529|lang=pt|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>Aguilar, A. M. G. C. 2013. ''Contribuições Etnolinguísticas e Histórico-Comparativas para os estudos sobre os povos e as línguas Kawahíwa''. Tese (Exame de Qualificação de Doutorado), PPGL/UnB.</ref>

Languages spoken in north-central [[Rondônia]] are Karipúna, Uru-eu-wau-wau (Jupaú), Amondawa, and unidentified varieties by some isolated groups. Languages spoken in northeastern [[Mato Grosso]] and southern [[Pará]] are Apiaká, Kayabí, Piripkúra, and unidentified varieties by some isolated groups.

Other Kawahíva dialects became extinct, the most recent being '''Capivara''' with the death of Pitanga Capivara in the fall 2022.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Nascimento dos Santos |first=Wesley |title=Topics on the syntax of Kawahíva: A Tupí-Guaraní language from the Brazilian Amazon |date=2024 |publisher=UC Berkeley |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1h26s7sq |language=en}}</ref> Other varieties include '''Paranawat''' at Machado/[[Ji-Paraná River]], '''Takwatip''' and '''Ipotewap''' at Muqui river, attested by [[Curt Nimuendajú|Nimuendajú]] and [[Claude Lévi-Strauss|Lévi-Strauss]] around the 1950s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lévi-Strauss |first=Claude |title=[[Tristes Tropiques]] |publisher=Librairie Plon |year=1955 |isbn=2-266-11982-6 |location=France, Brazil |language=fr |trans-title=Sad Tropics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Nimuendajú  |first=Curt |title=[[Handbook of South American Indians]] |edition=Steward, Julian H., ed. (1948) |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |pages=283-297 |year=1940–1947 |location=Washington, DC |language=en}}</ref> Lévi-Strauss also mentions people who were already almost extinct at that time, who lived near the Ji-Paraná river, like the '''Tucumanfét''' and the '''Jabotiféd'''; and the '''Mialat''', who inhabited the Leitão River region.
